newsitem.title: USA: Freshmen Republicans suffer few losses in election.
newsitem.headline: Freshmen Republicans suffer few losses in election.

text.p: Most of the Republican freshmen who swept their party into control of the House of Representatives two years ago survived this year's election despite a massive effort by Democrats and organised labour to unseat them.
With about 14 House races still undecided early on Wednesday, projected returns point to losses by no more than 15 of the 70 freshmen Republicans seeking re-election.

The freshmen were key to House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich's revolution and voted to keep the government shut down last January when even Gingrich had decided to compromise with President Bill Clinton on budget issues.
Labour unions targeted many of the freshmen in this year's election campaigns, spending millions of dollars on advertising to boost Democratic challengers.
In Michigan, Democrat Debbie Stabenow, one of those who got heavy labour support, defeated Republican Dick Chrysler and Democrat Walter Capps ousted Republican Andrea Seastrand in California.

In Washington, where six Republican freshmen won in 1994, Randy Tate was defeated by Democrat Adam Smith and Linda Smith and Jack Metcalf were trailing in races which were too close to call. But first-termers Rick White, Doc Hastings and George Nethercutt all won. Oregon freshman Jim Bunn was also trailing in another undecided race.

In Illinois, Republicans lost the Chicago seat held by Representative Michael Flanagan to Democrat Rod Blagojevich. Flanagan was dismissed by opponents as the "accidental congressman" who brought down veteran Democratic Representative Dan Rostenkowski who was under investigation for misuse of congressional funds. The district was heavily Democratic.

A strong stand for gun control gave New York Democrat Carolyn McCarthy a win over Republican Representative Dan Frisa. McCarthy's husband was killed in an attack by a gunman on a subway and her son suffered brain damage. She entered the race after Frisa refused to endorse gun control measures.
In Ohio, Democrat Ted Strickland pulled ahead of Republican Representative Frank Cremeans, 51 percent to 49 percent.
Two North Carolina freshman were upset.

Representative David Funderburk was one of the Democratic party's main targets and was projected to have lost to Democrat Bobby Etheridge, a state official. Funderburk faced charges that he had been the driver during an auto accident but switched seats to avoid blame. He had been politically allied with Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, who won a fifth term.

Representative Fred Heineman who represented the Raleigh-Chapel Hill area lost in a rematch with Democratic former Representative David Price who charged that the Republicans votes with Gingrich hurt the district.
New Jersey Representative Bill Martini, who won by the narrowest of margins in 1994, was turned out by Democrat William Pascrell whose campaign linked the Republican to Gingrich.

Representative James Longley of Maine, closely allied with Gingrich, lost to Democrat Tom Allen, a former mayor of Portland who said the Republican's views were too conservative for the district which had tended to elect moderates.
Republican National Committee chairman Haley Barbour said voters sent Washington a mixed message with the re-election of Clinton while Republicans held control of Congress.
But White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta told television networks the message was a call for bipartisan compromise on legislation.
"The American people, frankly, are sick of gridlock and partisanship and the kind of political attacks and personal attacks that we've seen," he said.

Three of the 73 freshmen Republicans did not seek re-election to the House. Sam Brownback was elected to the Senate from Kansas and Enid Greene of Utah and Wes Cooley of Oregon did not run due to scandals involving their 1994 campaigns, but Republicans held on to all three seats.
